Amounting
uh-MOWN-ting
v. (participle, = totaling, coming to a sum)
From Old French amonter (to ascend, to come up to), from mont (mountain); appearing once in the Authorized Version to state the total weight of gold overlaying the most holy place of Solomon's temple.

Biblical Definition

He overlaid it with fine gold, amounting to six hundred talents.

Amounting appears once in the Authorized Version, in Chronicles' account of the building of Solomon's temple, stating the precise total weight of gold used to overlay the most holy house — six hundred talents, an enormous sum by any ancient measure. The word does the simple arithmetical work of a total, but the number it totals is itself part of the text's larger argument: Chronicles takes evident care to record exact measurements and exact quantities of costly material throughout its temple-building narrative, underscoring that the house built for the LORD's name was not built cheaply or carelessly but at a cost commensurate with the glory of the One it was built to honour. Amounting to six hundred talents stands alongside other precise figures in the same chapters — cubits of length and breadth, numbers of pillars, weights of various fittings — as part of a deliberate rhetorical strategy: extravagant, exact, verifiable cost as a form of worship in itself, offered before a single sacrifice was made within the finished house.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from AMOUNT: to rise to, in the aggregate; to come to, as a sum total; here as the participle amounting, stating the total weight of gold used in Solomon's temple.

AMOUNT, v.i. To rise or swell to, in the aggregate; to come to, as a total sum.

AMOUNT, v.i. To result in, or be equivalent to, in substance or effect.

AMOUNTING, the present participle, here used of a total quantity reached.

In 2 Chronicles 3:8 the word states the precise weight of gold overlaying the most holy place.

Chronicles records exact quantities throughout its temple-building narrative as a mark of costly devotion.

Key Scripture

2Ch 3:8 — "And he made the most holy house, the length whereof was according to the breadth of the house, twenty cubits, and the breadth thereof twenty cubits: and he overlaid it with fine gold, amounting to six hundred talents."

Modern Corruption

There is no live postmodern redefinition of this ordinary arithmetical word; the entry exists because its single occurrence names a precise, extravagant cost that Chronicles records deliberately, as an argument that worship rightly costs something real.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Amounting retains its plain arithmetical sense; no rival ideology has captured the word.

The principle to recover is the chapter's own implicit argument: Chronicles does not summarize the temple's cost in general terms but insists on the exact figure, six hundred talents, amounting to a sum meant to be felt as extravagant. Precise, costly devotion is treated in this narrative as itself a form of worship, offered in materials before it is offered in sacrifice.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Amounting occurs once, in Chronicles' precise accounting of the gold used to overlay Solomon's most holy place, part of a broader pattern of exact measurement throughout the temple-building narrative.

expand to see more

Amounting in 2 Chronicles 3:8 states the total weight of gold overlaying the most holy place.

The figure given, six hundred talents, is an enormous sum by ancient measure.

Chronicles pairs this figure with exact cubit measurements of length and breadth.

The parallel account in 1 Kings 6 describes the same overlaying without this specific total.

The temple's costly materials are gathered in large part from David's own prior provision.

Usage

"Amounting to six hundred talents — a precise, extravagant total recorded deliberately."

"He overlaid it with fine gold — costly material offered before a single sacrifice was made."

"Chronicles' exact figures form part of its argument that worship rightly costs something real."
